source_title: The More You Buy, The More You Lose
other_side: This edition's premise is that token spend is a management problem — spend wisely, measure cost per accepted task, and the arithmetic comes good. Zitron, five days earlier, argued that the arithmetic does not come good at any level of discipline, because the price you are quoted is not the cost of the thing. His evidence is that heavy usage destroys the seller, not the buyer: Anthropic and OpenAI, he writes, "allow users to burn $8000 to $14,000 a month for $200", and GitHub Copilot only reached scale by letting subscribers "burn more than 25 times their monthly subscription fee" — with user revolts when metered billing arrived. He notes that NVIDIA's promised twenty-five-fold cut in inference cost has been quietly pared back to ten, and that even that has made no AI company profitable. His conclusion is that "using AI only seems to be getting more expensive" for everyone in the chain, and that a cost-per-accepted-task discipline optimises a number that is subsidised in the first place.
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether the price of a unit of AI work reflects what it costs to produce. They agree on more than the framing suggests — tokens are opaque, agentic work multiplies consumption several-fold, and the heaviest users pay a small fraction of what they consume. The empirical question that will resolve is whether inference gets cheap enough to be simultaneously profitable to sell and worth buying; the observable that settles it is published inference gross margins and whether the flat-rate heavy-use plans survive without conversion to metered billing. The residue is pure worldview: whether discipline is the answer or the distraction. Whittemore is vindicated if measured cost per accepted task falls while capability holds and vendors still make money. Zitron is vindicated if the subsidy is withdrawn and the true price makes the work uneconomic. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both now say the sticker price tells you nothing. Watch whether flat-rate plans quietly become metered.
